messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malik, a 22-year-old school principal in a small district office on the edge of a busy African immigrant neighborhood, came to treatment after months of feeling as though the past was pressing into the present from every direction. He had grown up with a caregiver who beat him as a child, often in abrupt bursts that left no warning and no explanation, and he now described his world as being organized around the fear of the next unpredictable blow. What made the memories especially potent was not just the abuse itself but how they returned: old photos could stop him cold, and waking from a nightmare would leave him disoriented and on edge, as if he had been yanked back into an old room he could not quite see. In those moments, the event did not come back to him as a smooth story; it arrived in disconnected pieces that did not fit together, and because he could not deliberately pull the memory into a clear sequence when he tried, he was left with fragments that felt more real and vivid than ordinary memories, sharp enough to make him distrust what he was seeing around him.

The more Malik found himself caught by those fragments, the more he came to believe that something had been permanently altered in him. He would sit at his desk in the school office, looking over disciplinary reports or fielding sudden interruptions from staff, and the smallest unpredictability in the day could pull him into the same conclusion: he could not stop bad things from happening to him. A student arriving in tears without warning, a parent demanding to speak immediately, even a change in the schedule he had not anticipated could make his chest tighten with the old sense of helplessness. Because the memories came back in broken pieces, he struggled to place them safely in the past, and that uncertainty fed his fear that he had changed for the worse. He had come to believe that if he were pushed enough, his own anger might become dangerous; he worried that he would not be able to control it and would do something terrible. That fear did not stay abstract. When the memories felt especially vivid, he became more watchful for anything that might set him off, and he found himself bracing against ordinary moments, scanning faces and voices for signs that another blow, humiliation, or loss of control might be coming.

As the months went by, those fears shaped what Malik allowed himself to encounter. Old photographs were no longer casual reminders of family or childhood; he avoided looking through albums, and he would ask his partner to put away pictures from family gatherings if they surfaced on a phone screen. When his own mind felt unstable, he interpreted the old photos as evidence that the injured child was still present inside him, unchanged in the worst way, and that made the memories feel even more vivid and threatening. The nightmares had the same effect. He dreaded waking suddenly in the night because the residue of the dream made him feel as if something bad was about to happen, and by morning he was already prepared for danger. In the school building, unpredictable situations became increasingly hard to tolerate, so he began stepping back from hallway conflicts and delegating more than he used to, not because he lacked competence but because he feared what his body and mind might do under pressure. Yet every attempt to steady himself seemed to circle back into the same experience: the more he tried to keep the memory in order, the more it broke apart; the more it broke apart, the more convinced he became that he was damaged and at risk; and the more convinced he became, the more tightly he avoided the things that might remind him of it.

By the time he sought help, Malik was exhausted by how much space the fear had taken up in his work and his relationship. He cared deeply about his partner and wanted to stay present, but he was frightened that his irritability and constant anticipation of danger would spill into the people he loved or into the school community that relied on him. What finally brought him in was a night of waking from a nightmare and finding himself unable to settle, then spending the next day moving through the office with the old familiar sense that he could not stop bad things from happening. He hopes to understand why the memories remain so raw and why old photos, unexpected disruptions, and the shock of waking from dreams can still make him feel as though he is back in the hands of that childhood violence, and he is most afraid that the version of himself shaped by it will stay permanently in control.
